analysis.one_liner: Makes lobbyist payments to Members of Congress a federal bribery crime.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had no cosponsors, never received a committee vote and died when the 103rd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Representative Andrew Jacobs Jr. proposed that any payment of money or anything of value from a professional lobbyist or lobbying organization to a Senator or Representative, or on their behalf, be treated as bribery under federal criminal law. The bill went to the House Judiciary Committee, then to its crime subcommittee, and no further action was ever taken on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary citizens who want a stricter criminal backstop on the money that flows from professional lobbying organizations to the people who write federal legislation. Members of Congress who accept no lobbyist payments also gain a clearer rule of the road.

how_it_helps.text: Under the bill, any payment of money or other thing of value to, or on behalf of, a Senator or Representative from a professional lobbying organization or individual professional lobbyist for legislation would constitute bribery under federal criminal law [S3].
The measure was aimed squarely at congressional ethics, with listed subjects including bribery, congressional ethics, lobbying, and Members of Congress [S1].

analysis.who_pays: Professional lobbying organizations and individual lobbyists, who would face criminal exposure for payments to Members, and Members of Congress, who could face bribery charges for accepting them.

drawbacks.text: The bill's definition is sweeping: it does not carve out campaign contributions, so ordinary political donations from lobbyists and lobbying organizations to Members could be swept into the same federal bribery offense as outright bribes, raising questions about how the law would interact with legal campaign finance [S3].

Existing federal bribery and gift rules already prohibit quid pro quo payments and restrict gifts, so critics could argue this bill overlaps with existing law rather than closing a demonstrated gap [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea — putting lobbyists' payments to lawmakers under the same criminal standard as bribery — is a clear, enforceable rule that targets a widely criticized practice. But as written, the bill is a single broad sentence with no exception for campaign contributions, so an honest supporter would acknowledge it needed refinement before it could become workable law. It never got that refinement.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then to its crime subcommittee on February 10, 1993, and no vote or further action ever happened before the Congress ended [S5].

narrative.text: Representative Andrew Jacobs Jr., a Democrat from Indiana, introduced the bill on January 5, 1993, the opening day of the 103rd Congress [S1] [S5].
It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on the day of introduction and then to the Subcommittee on Crime and Criminal Justice on February 10, 1993 [S5].
The bill attracted no cosponsors during the entire two-year Congress [S4].
No committee markup, floor vote, or further action was ever recorded; the bill died in subcommittee when the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Lobbyists and Members of Congress remain able to exchange payments without the payments themselves being a federal bribery offense under this provision; the bill's death left the existing bribery and gift rules unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Lobbyists and the Members they pay

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, and the bill drew no cosponsors from either party, so no partisan division was ever tested [S4] [S5].

industries.note: The bill would make any payment from a lobbyist or lobbying organization to a Member of Congress, or on a Member's behalf, a federal bribery crime, ending the practice as a legal gray area. Their interest in blocking it ran against the public's interest in clean lawmaking [S3].

Members could have faced bribery charges for accepting lobbyist payments, including payments made on their behalf. The bill's failure to attract any cosponsors came from the very body it would have regulated [S3] [S4].
